Introduction¶

In this report, I have created several visualisations to illustrate the history and impact of major earthquakes around the world, with a specific focus on Indonesia. This region is notably frequent in experiencing high-magnitude earthquakes, making it a critical area of study. By employing data from two primary sources, including the pivotal earthquakes.usgs API known for its accurate earthquake data, these visualisations aim to highlight global earthquake hotspots and delve into Indonesia's seismic activity.

Visualisations Overview¶

1. World Earthquake Map (2D)

  • A basic 2D map showcasing all major earthquakes worldwide since 2000. This visualisation provides a straightforward overview of earthquake distribution on a global scale.

2. Interactive Global Earthquake Globe (3D)

  • An enhanced 3D interactive globe featuring the same earthquake data as the 2D map, augmented with tectonic plates overlays. This visualisation offers a dynamic and immersive exploration of the Earth's seismic activity.

3. Indonesia Earthquake Map (Interactive)

  • Focusing on Indonesia, this interactive map highlights major earthquakes within the region over a more extended timescale. It also includes tectonic plates mapping and annotations for the specific year of each earthquake, offering a detailed local perspective.

4. Global Earthquake Distribution (3D Scatter Plot)

  • A 3D scatter plot visualising the distribution of earthquakes from 1990 onwards, covering a broader range of magnitudes. This visualisation aims to convey the overall frequency and impact of seismic events globally.

5. Indonesia Earthquake Intensity Map (2.5D)

  • Utilising a 2.5D map, this visualisation depicts earthquakes in Indonesia from 1990 onwards as 3D bars. It effectively highlights the most significant seismic events, offering clear insight into their magnitude and impact.

Through these visualisations, this report endeavours to shed light on the patterns and hotspots of seismic activity, particularly emphasising the frequent and high-magnitude earthquakes in Indonesia. The combination of detailed research and accurate data aims to provide a comprehensive understanding of global and regional earthquake trends.

Mapping All Major World Earthquakes¶

This section aims to visually represent all major earthquakes (magnitude 7 or higher) globally from the year 2000 to the current year. The design emphasizes areas significantly affected by severe seismic activities, highlighting the distribution and frequency of these major earthquakes worldwide.

Utilizing data from the USGS Earthquake Catalog API, this map provides a comprehensive and reliable source for real-time and historical earthquake data. The API's advanced filtering capabilities allow for precise selection of earthquake events by magnitude, time, and geographic location, ensuring the visualization's accuracy and relevance.

"Magnitude is the size of the earthquake...each whole number increase in magnitude represents a tenfold increase in measured amplitude as measured on a seismogram." This insight is crucial for understanding the impact of earthquakes [2].

Data for this map was fetched through a request to the USGS API for earthquakes with a magnitude of 7 or higher, spanning from the year 2000 until the current year. The visual representation employs simple red circles to indicate earthquake occurrences, where the size of each circle may correspond to the earthquake's magnitude. The map is designed for interactive use, allowing users to zoom and pan to explore different regions in greater detail. Clicking on the circles reveals additional information, such as the specific earthquake's magnitude, providing users with a more detailed understanding of each seismic event. vent.

In [2]:
# the time period for the data
start = 2000
present = datetime.now().year  # current year

# Fetching data from USGS Earthquake API for years 2000-2020 with magnitude over 7
url = f"https://earthquake.usgs.gov/fdsnws/event/1/query?format=geojson&starttime={start}-01-01&endtime={present}-12-31&minmagnitude=7&limit=1000"
# reference [3]
response = requests.get(url)
earthquake_data = response.json()
In [3]:
# constructing a simple 2d map with folium just plotting the map of the eargthquake data
map = folium.Map(location=[0, 0], zoom_start=2)

# Add earthquakes to the map
for quake in earthquake_data['features']:
    location = quake['geometry']['coordinates'][1], quake['geometry']['coordinates'][0]
    magnitude = quake['properties']['mag']
    folium.CircleMarker(
        location=location,
        radius=magnitude * 2,  # Adjust the size scaling as needed
        popup=f"Magnitude: {magnitude}\nLocation: {location}", # creates a simple location and magnitude popup
        color='red',
        fill=True,
        fill_color='red'
    ).add_to(map)

# Display the map
map

Understanding the Pattern of Major Earthquakes¶

Upon examining the map of major earthquakes, it becomes evident that these seismic events are not randomly distributed. Instead, they are clustered in specific regions, while other areas remain unaffected. This observation raises an intriguing question: why do some areas repeatedly experience earthquakes of magnitude 7 or higher, while others never do? To delve deeper, we must consider aspects not visible on this map.

A crucial factor in understanding earthquake distribution is tectonic plates. The movement and interaction of these plates are fundamental to seismic activity. Therefore, in our next visualisation, we will incorporate tectonic plate boundaries alongside the existing earthquake data. This addition aims to provide a clearer understanding of the disruptive boundaries that contribute to the occurrence of significant seismic events.

For this enhanced visualisation, we will source data on tectonic plate boundaries from the ArcGIS[4] API. Including this information will allow us to better comprehend the underlying causes of earthquake patterns, offering insights into the areas most susceptible to high-magnitude earthquakes.

In [4]:
# tectonic data 
url = "https://services.arcgis.com/jIL9msH9OI208GCb/arcgis/rest/services/Tectonic_Plates_and_Boundaries/FeatureServer/0/query" # Reference [4]
params = {'where': '1=1','outFields': '*','outSR': '4326','f': 'geojson'}
response = requests.get(url, params=params)

tectonic_data = response.json()

Earthquakes and Tectonic Plate Boundaries on 3D Globe¶

Our upcoming visualisation takes a comprehensive approach by overlaying earthquake data onto a map of tectonic plate boundaries. This method aims to provide a clear visual correlation between the location of tectonic plates and the occurrence of earthquakes. Here’s how the visualisation is constructed:

  • Tectonic Plate Boundaries: Mapped with clarity, these boundaries delineate the edges of major tectonic plates. Understanding these boundaries is key to grasping why certain areas are more prone to seismic activities.

  • Earthquake Data: Positioned accurately on the map, each earthquake is represented by a circle. The size of the circle correlates with the earthquake's magnitude—the larger the circle, the higher the magnitude. This sizing provides an immediate visual indicator of the earthquake's strength.

  • Colour Scale: Adds an additional layer of information to the visualisation. The colour of each circle will vary according to the magnitude of the earthquake, offering a quick visual reference to assess the severity of each event.

This visualisation strategy not only makes it easier to identify the most seismically active regions but also allows us to observe the relationship between tectonic plate boundaries and earthquake magnitudes. By integrating a colour scale with the size variation of the circles, users can quickly gauge the magnitude and significance of each seismic event, offering a deeper understanding of global earthquake patterns.

In [5]:
# Extract latitude, longitude, and magnitude of earthquakes
lats = [quake['geometry']['coordinates'][1] for quake in earthquake_data['features']]
lons = [quake['geometry']['coordinates'][0] for quake in earthquake_data['features']]
mags = [quake['properties']['mag'] for quake in earthquake_data['features']]

# Initialize a figure
fig = go.Figure()

# Plot tectonic plates
for feature in tectonic_data['features']:
    if feature['geometry']['type'] == 'LineString':
        coordinates = feature['geometry']['coordinates']
        lons_plates, lats_plates = zip(*coordinates)  # Unzip the list of [lon, lat] pairs into two lists

        fig.add_trace(go.Scattergeo(
            lon=lons_plates,
            lat=lats_plates,
            mode='lines',
            line=dict(width=1, color='blue'),
            hoverinfo='skip' 
        ))
    elif feature['geometry']['type'] == 'MultiLineString':
        for segment in feature['geometry']['coordinates']:
            lons_plates, lats_plates = zip(*segment)
            fig.add_trace(go.Scattergeo(
                lon=lons_plates,
                lat=lats_plates,
                mode='lines',
                line=dict(width=1, color='blue'),
                hoverinfo='skip'
            ))

# Plot earthquakes
fig.add_trace(go.Scattergeo(
    lon=lons,
    lat=lats,
    text=[f'Magnitude: {mag}' for mag in mags],
    mode='markers',
    marker = dict(
        size = [10 * (mag - 5) for mag in mags],  # Scale magnitude for visibility
        opacity = 0.8,
        color = mags,
        colorscale = 'Reds',
        cmin = min(mags),
        cmax = max(mags),
        colorbar_title = "Magnitude",
        line = dict(width=1, color='rgba(102, 102, 102)')
    )
))

# Configure the layout for a 3D globe projection
fig.update_geos(
    projection_type = "orthographic",
    showland = True,
    landcolor = "rgb(212, 212, 212)",
    showocean = True,
    oceancolor = "rgb(10, 125, 255)",
    showcountries = True,  # Optionally add countries for better context
)

# Update layout
fig.update_layout(
    title='Global Earthquakes with Magnitude 7 or More (2000-2020) and Tectonic Plates',
    showlegend=False,
    width=1000,  # Adjusted for better visibility
    height=800,
)

fig.show()

Focusing on Indonesia: Visualising Major Earthquakes¶

To delve into the seismic activity within Indonesia, we tailor our approach to provide a focused visualisation. This segment is dedicated to mapping earthquakes of magnitude 7 or higher in Indonesia, leveraging data from 1970 to the present. Here's how we proceed:

  • Setting the Coordinates: We begin by pinpointing the geographical coordinates of Indonesia. This step ensures that our visualisation is centred around the region of interest, providing a clear and detailed view of seismic activity.

  • 2D Folium Map: The visualisation is presented as a 2D Folium map, chosen for its ability to render interactive and highly detailed maps. This tool allows us to effectively display significant earthquakes within Indonesia's boundaries.

  • Data Range (1970-Present): The choice of timeframe, spanning the last half-century, is deliberate. It balances the need for a sufficiently long period to analyse high-magnitude earthquakes (7+) against the desire for data reliability and relevance. While earthquakes of magnitude 5-6 are relatively common in Indonesia, those of magnitude 7 or higher are rarer. By selecting this timescale, we aim to highlight these significant events without extending so far back that data reliability becomes a concern.

  • Magnitude 7+ Earthquakes: Focusing on earthquakes of this magnitude allows for a clear analysis of seismic events that have had a substantial impact on the region. The map will showcase these earthquakes, providing insights into their frequency, distribution, and potential patterns over the past fifty years.

This Indonesia-specific visualisation serves as a crucial component of our study, offering a detailed examination of major seismic activity within a region that is frequently affected by earthquakes. By analysing data from the past half-century, we gain valuable perspectives on the occurrence and impact of high-magnitude earthquakes in Indonesia.

In [14]:
# Define the geographical boundaries of Indonesia
minlatitude = -11.0  # southern boundary
maxlatitude = 6.0    # northern boundary
minlongitude = 95.0  # western boundary
maxlongitude = 141.0  # eastern boundary

# Fetch data from USGS Earthquake API for years 2000-2020 with magnitude over 7
url = f"https://earthquake.usgs.gov/fdsnws/event/1/query?format=geojson&starttime=1970-01-01&endtime={present}-12-31&minmagnitude=7&minlatitude={minlatitude}&maxlatitude={maxlatitude}&minlongitude={minlongitude}&maxlongitude={maxlongitude}&limit=1000"
response = requests.get(url)
earthquake_data = response.json()

Indonesia Earthquake Map Description¶

Our next visualisation presents a focused examination of seismic activity within Indonesia, depicted on a 2D map. This map is specifically designed to offer insights into the largest earthquakes occurring in the region from 1970 to the present. Below are the key features and design choices of this map:

  • 2D Map Basis: The foundation of this visualisation is a 2D map, chosen for its clarity and ease of interpretation. This format allows for the effective display of geographic and seismic data in a manner that is accessible to a wide audience.

  • Tectonic Plate Boundaries: An essential component of this map is the delineation of tectonic plate boundaries. These are accurately mapped to provide context for the seismic events, illustrating the relationship between tectonic movements and earthquake occurrences in Indonesia.

  • Indonesia-Specific Data: The map focuses on displaying a comprehensive dataset of major earthquakes within Indonesia, highlighting the most significant seismic events since 1970. This focus ensures that the visualisation is rich with region-specific insights.

  • Circle Markers: Each earthquake is represented by a circle marker on the map. These markers not only pinpoint the location of the earthquake but also convey additional information, such as the year the earthquake occurred. This multi-dimensional representation allows users to quickly grasp the temporal distribution of seismic events.

  • Customised View: The map is carefully zoomed and panned to fit the geographical bounds of Indonesia, ensuring that the entire region is in view. This tailored presentation maximises the relevance and usability of the map for viewers interested in Indonesia's seismic activity.

By combining detailed earthquake data with tectonic boundary information and a region-specific focus, this map provides a valuable tool for analysing the historical pattern and impact of significant earthquakes in Indonesia. The visualisation aims to offer a comprehensive overview of seismic activity, with a clear emphasis on the most impactful events over the last five decades.

In [15]:
# Calculate average latitude and longitude for the center of the map
avg_lat = (minlatitude + maxlatitude) / 2
avg_lon = (minlongitude + maxlongitude) / 2

map = folium.Map(location=[avg_lat, avg_lon], zoom_start=5)

# Add tectonic plate boundaries to the map
folium.GeoJson(
    tectonic_data,
    name='tectonic_plates',
    style_function=lambda x: {'color': 'blue', 'weight': 2, 'fillColor': 'transparent'}
).add_to(map)

# Add earthquakes to the map
for quake in earthquake_data['features']:
    location = (quake['geometry']['coordinates'][1], quake['geometry']['coordinates'][0])
    magnitude = quake['properties']['mag']
    year = datetime.utcfromtimestamp(quake['properties']['time'] / 1000).strftime('%Y')
    # Add more to pop-up
    popup_html = f"""
    <div>
        <h5>Earthquake Details:</h5>
        <p><strong>Magnitude:</strong> {magnitude}</p>
        <p><strong>Year:</strong> {year}</p>
    </div>
    """
    folium.CircleMarker(
        location=location,
        radius=magnitude * 2,  # Adjust the size scaling as needed
        popup=folium.Popup(popup_html, max_width=300),
        color='red',
        fill=True,
        fill_color='red'
    ).add_to(map)

# Add a layer control panel to the map
folium.LayerControl().add_to(map)

# Display the map in Jupyter Notebook (if you are using one)
map

Advanced Analysis: Earthquakes in Indonesia (1990-Present)¶

In this section, we delve deeper into the seismic activity of Indonesia, expanding our analysis to include all earthquakes of magnitude 5 and above from 1990 to the present. This approach allows us to capture a more nuanced understanding of the region's seismic risks and the extreme magnitudes that some earthquakes reach. Here’s the rationale and methodology for this advanced analysis:

Focus on Magnitude 5+ Earthquakes¶

  • Magnitude 4 and Below: Earthquakes with a magnitude of 4 or lower, while frequent in Indonesia, are generally not destructive and thus offer limited insight into the seismic hazards faced by the region.

  • Magnitude 5 and Above: By starting our analysis at magnitude 5, we can focus on earthquakes that have the potential to cause significant damage. This threshold ensures that our visualisation captures the more impactful seismic events, providing a clearer picture of the earthquake risks in Indonesia.

Data Acquisition¶

  • Calling the Data: The first step in this analysis is to acquire the relevant earthquake data. This involves making a request to our primary data source (presumably the USGS Earthquake Catalog API or a similar comprehensive earthquake database) for records of all earthquakes in the Indonesia region with a magnitude of 5 or higher, spanning from 1990 to the present.

Visualisation Strategy¶

  • Upcoming Visualisations: Armed with this more precise dataset, we will construct visualisations that not only highlight the locations of these earthquakes but also illustrate the range and severity of magnitudes experienced. This approach aims to shed light on the frequency of significant seismic events in Indonesia and the potential for extreme magnitudes.

This final section of our analysis is designed to offer a comprehensive overview of Indonesia's earthquake activity over the last three decades, emphasizing the seismic events that pose the greatest risk to the region. By focusing on earthquakes of magnitude 5 and above, we aim to provide a more detailed and relevant perspective on the patterns and potential dangers of seismic activity in Indonesia.

In [11]:
# Define the time period
start = 1990
#end_year is already sset to present at the start

# Fetch Earthquake Data
url = f"https://earthquake.usgs.gov/fdsnws/event/1/query?format=geojson&starttime={start}-01-01&endtime={present}-12-31&minlatitude=-11&maxlatitude=6&minlongitude=95&maxlongitude=141&minmagnitude=5&limit=10000"
response = requests.get(url)

data = response.json()

# Prepare the Data
earthquakes = []
for feature in data['features']:
    props = feature['properties']
    geom = feature['geometry']
    earthquakes.append({
        'Magnitude': props['mag'],
        'Longitude': geom['coordinates'][0],
        'Latitude': geom['coordinates'][1],
    })

df = pd.DataFrame(earthquakes)

3D Scatter Plot: Earthquake Magnitudes and Distribution in Indonesia¶

Our journey through seismic analysis culminates with a striking 3D scatter plot that brings to life the distribution and magnitudes of earthquakes in Indonesia. This visualisation doesn't just plot points on a map; it offers a deep dive into the heart of Indonesia's seismic activities. Here's why this particular visual stands out:

What Sets It Apart¶

  • Depth and Perspective: The 3D aspect of this scatter plot doesn't just add aesthetic value; it provides a richer, more nuanced view of seismic activity. You get to see the full scope of how earthquakes spread across the region, with the plot's depth adding a layer of understanding to the magnitude and distribution of these events.

  • Size and Colour Coding: Each earthquake's magnitude is visually represented, making it straightforward to spot the more severe quakes. Larger, more vividly coloured markers point out the bigger tremors, quickly drawing your attention to the areas at greater risk. [5]

  • Spotting the Patterns: This visualisation is also a tool for spotting patterns. A cluster of large markers signals a hotspot of seismic activity, offering insights into where big quakes are more likely to occur.

Insights Offered¶

  • A Clear View on Magnitude: This plot makes it easy to pick out the most significant quakes. It provides a unique vantage point, letting you gauge the scale of seismic events in Indonesia at a glance.

  • Understanding Earthquake Density: Beyond just mapping, this visualisation clarifies the density of quakes of various magnitudes. It highlights the areas more prone to intense seismic activity, underlining the regions that could be considered seismic danger zones.

In short, this 3D scatter plot is an invaluable tool for delving into Indonesia's seismic landscape. It offers a vivid, comprehensive view that enhances our understanding of earthquake risks across the region. By bringing data to life in three dimensions, it unveils patterns and details that could easily be missed in simpler, two-dimensional representations.

In [12]:
# Create a 3D scatter plot of the earthquake data using Plotly
fig = go.Figure(data=[go.Scatter3d(
    x=df['Longitude'],
    y=df['Latitude'],
    z=df['Magnitude'],
    mode='markers',
    marker=dict(
        size=4,  # Adjust size of markers
        color=df['Magnitude'],  # Set color to represent magnitude
        colorscale='Jet',  # Changed color scale here
        colorbar=dict(title='Magnitude'),
        opacity=0.8
    )
)])

# Set the layout of the figure
fig.update_layout(
    title='Indonesia Earthquake Data (1990 - Present)',
    scene=dict(
        xaxis=dict(title='Longitude'),
        yaxis=dict(title='Latitude'),
        zaxis=dict(title='Magnitude'),
    ),
    autosize=False,
    width=800,
    height=600,
    margin=dict(l=50, r=50, b=100, t=100),
)

fig.show()

Visualisation: 2.5D Bar Map of Earthquake Magnitudes in Indonesia¶

We wrap up our analysis with a striking visualisation that brings earthquake magnitudes in Indonesia to life using 3D bars. This creative approach doesn’t just list numbers; it uses bar height and colour to quantify earthquake magnitudes and places them on the map to show their geographical locations. Here's a snapshot of what makes this visualisation stand out:

Highlights¶

  • 3D Bars: Each bar symbolises an earthquake, where the height reflects its magnitude. This method vividly illustrates how severe each earthquake was.

  • Colour Gradient: The bars change colour based on the earthquake's magnitude, offering an intuitive grasp of the event's intensity. Brighter colours signal stronger earthquakes.

  • Geographical Layout: We’ve placed the bars to match their real-world locations, making it easy to spot Indonesia's seismic hotspots.

Interactions and Insights¶

  • Spotting Seismic Hotspots: The tallest, brightest bars point out where the most devastating earthquakes hit, quickly showing which areas are most at risk.

  • Dive Deeper with a Hover: Moving your cursor over the bars pulls up details like magnitude, inviting you to explore each earthquake more closely.

This 2.5D bar chart is more than just a visualisation; it’s a gateway to understanding the scale and distribution of earthquakes in Indonesia. By blending 3D presentation with colour-coded magnitudes and interactive elements, it delivers a comprehensive look at seismic activity, underscoring the regions most affected. It’s a visually engaging way to compare earthquake magnitudes and locations, revealing deep insights into Indonesia’s seismic landscape.

In [13]:
def get_color_by_magnitude(magnitude):
    if magnitude < 5.4:
        return [0, 0, 0, 140]  # Black, representing the lowest severity
    elif magnitude < 5.8:
        return [111, 0, 255, 140]  # Dark Purple, for emerging severity
    elif magnitude < 6.2:
        return [214, 40, 0, 140]  # Dark Red, indicating increasing concern
    elif magnitude < 6.6:
        return [255, 109, 0, 140]  # Bright Orange, marking caution
    elif magnitude < 7:
        return [255, 173, 0, 140]   # Light Orange, for heightened alertness
    elif magnitude < 8:
        return [255, 255, 0, 140]    # Yellow, signaling high severity
    else:
        return [255, 255, 255, 140]  # White, for the utmost severity and urgency

# Apply the color mapping function to the dataframe
df['color'] = df['Magnitude'].apply(get_color_by_magnitude)

# Define a Column Layer with adjusted height to reflect earthquake magnitude and dynamic color coding
column_layer = pdk.Layer(
    "ColumnLayer",
    data=df,
    get_position=["Longitude", "Latitude"],
    get_elevation="(Magnitude-4.5) * 1000",  # Adjust magnitude representation in elevation
    radius=4000,  # Adjust radius size here if needed
    elevation_scale=100,  # Adjusted for taller bars
    get_color="color",  # Use the dynamically assigned color
    pickable=True,
    elevation_range=[50, 5000],  # Extended range for better visualization
    extruded=True,
)

# Set the viewport location to focus on Indonesia
view_state = pdk.ViewState(
    longitude=118,
    latitude=-2.5,
    zoom=4,
    pitch=40.5,
    bearing=-27.36
)

# Render
r = pdk.Deck(
    layers=[column_layer],
    initial_view_state=view_state,
    tooltip={"text": "Magnitude: {Magnitude}"}
)

# Display the deck.gl map in Jupyter or save it to an HTML file
r.to_html('earthquake_column_layer_indonesia_magnitude_dynamic_color.html')

# code from Deck.gl Hexagon Layer documentation. Available at: https://deckgl.readthedocs.io/en/latest/gallery/hexagon_layer.html [7]
